title: A Plea to Restore a Ruined Vine
overview: A community in crisis begs God, pictured as a shepherd and a vine grower, to stop being angry and bring them back to life.

parts.label: Calling the Shepherd (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Joseph here stands for his descendants, the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, named alongside Benjamin, the tribe of Joseph's full brother; in the wilderness these three marched just behind the sacred tent. God is pictured enthroned above the cherubim, carved winged figures over the sacred chest, and is asked to shine out and wake up his strength.

parts.label: The repeated chorus (v. 3)
parts.note: "Make your face shine on us" echoes Israel's old priestly blessing and means "look on us with favor again." This plea returns in verses 7 and 19, naming God more fully each time.

parts.label: How long? (vv. 4-7)
parts.note: The people feel God is angry even at their prayers, so tears have become their daily bread and drink. Their neighbors quarrel over them like easy prey, and their enemies laugh.

parts.label: The vine from Egypt (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: Israel is pictured as a vine God brought out of Egypt and planted in Canaan after driving out the nations who lived there. It spread from the Mediterranean Sea to the Euphrates River, the widest borders Israel ever claimed.

parts.label: The vineyard torn down (vv. 12-16)
parts.note: Now the walls are broken, passersby strip the grapes and wild boars trample the vine, a picture of invasion that the poem says God himself allowed. Many scholars link this to Assyrian attacks on the northern kingdom in the 700s BC, though the exact event is uncertain.

parts.label: Prayer for a chosen one (vv. 17-19)
parts.note: "The man at your right hand" most likely means Israel's king or the nation itself, which verse 15 also calls a son God raised up, and the people promise to stay faithful if God revives them. Christians have also read this "son of man" in light of Jesus, who used that title for himself.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether "the man at your right hand" in verse 17 refers only to Israel's king or people, or also points ahead to Jesus.
think: When something you once loved has fallen apart, what makes it hard or possible to keep hoping it can be restored?
